Every node has exactly three neighbors." width="100%"} LCF notation (after Lederberg, Coxeter, and Frucht) describes a cubic Hamiltonian graph compactly. Place `n` nodes on a cycle `0, 1, ..., n-1`, then walk around it applying the list of `shifts=` over and over, `repeats=` times in all: the `j`-th shift `s` joins node `j mod n` to node `(j + s) mod n`. For example, the Heawood graph is `[5, -5]^7` (14 nodes, `shifts=[5, -5]`, `repeats=7`) and the cube is `[3, -3]^4`. A chord that duplicates an existing edge (or joins a node to itself) is skipped, so notation that is not exactly cubic still gives a simple graph. Nodes are created in cycle order, and in a directed graph every edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Many of the graphs in `add_named_graph()` are built this way. LCF notation is useful for: - entering cubic graphs from the literature, where they are often given in this form - building families of symmetric cubic graphs by varying the shifts - test cases for Hamiltonicity and cubic-graph algorithms ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes on the cycle. Must be at least `3`. [shifts]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The chord offsets, applied in order around the cycle, e.g. `[5, -5]`. Each is taken modulo `n=`; negative values count backward. An empty list gives just the cycle. [repeats]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How many times to apply the whole list of shifts. Default is `1`. For a cubic graph, `len(shifts) * repeats` equals `n=`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is less than `3` or `repeats=` is negative. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `[5, -5]^7` is the Heawood graph: 14 nodes, every node of degree `3`, and shortest cycle of length `6`: ::: {#e78d3b81 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_lcf_graph(n=14, shifts=[5, -5], repeats=7) graph.count_edges(), graph.girth(), graph.is_isomorphic( ec.Graph().add_named_graph("heawood") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (21, 6, True) ``` ::: ::: `[3, -3]^4` on eight nodes gives the cube: ::: {#39944aa5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} cube = ec.Graph().add_lcf_graph(n=8, shifts=[3, -3], repeats=4) cube.is_isomorphic(ec.Graph().add_hypercube_graph(d=3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
